slides.title: Horus connector assessment
slides.kicker: Chift product/tech case · Part 1 · Mapping Chift – Horus
slides.lead: Can Chift's accounting routes be served from the Horus Software API, and what must be confirmed before building?

items.text: Prepared by Silas Deblanc for Chift, Product & Tech
13 October 2026 · Status: for discussion
Basis: desk analysis of the documentation, no live API calls

slides.callout: Proposals are analysis, not commitments on behalf of Chift or Horus.
slides.notes: Thanks for having me. In about twenty minutes I'll cover four things. First, the answer: what the documentation confirms and what it doesn't. Second, how Horus differs from Chift, because most of the work comes from those differences. Third, Task A, the route mapping, and Task B, the attribute mapping for client creation, invoice creation and outstanding items. Finally, what your clients would notice, the decisions that are yours, the questions for Horus, and my recommendation. This is a desk analysis: no live API calls were sent, and anything I call a proposal is mine to discuss, not an agreed rule. Questions are welcome at the end.

slides.title: The case asked for route and attribute mappings, explained for clients
slides.lead: Two levels of mapping, built with the same method for every route.

items.text: Horus endpoints and specificities for 10 Chift routes
Every attribute and query parameter of 3 routes
One Chift route may need several Horus endpoints
Explain the result so Chift's clients can follow it, in plain language

blocks.heading: Method, the same for every route

items.text: Read both contracts in full for the routes in scope
Align vocabulary: each Chift term and its Horus equivalent
Ask the same questions per route: object, calls, fields, what is lost
Label every claim: Documented, Derived, Assumption, To confirm
Check each mapping against the docs, then challenge it in a critical review

slides.callout: Sources: the case, Chift OpenAPI spec (SDK 0.6.16), Horus reference (72 pages) and 15 guides, two VAT spreadsheets · desk analysis, no live API calls
slides.notes: The case asked two things. Task A: for ten Chift routes, which Horus endpoints to use and what to watch. Task B: for three routes, client creation, invoice creation and outstanding items, every attribute and query parameter. It also hinted that one Chift route may need several Horus calls, and that turned out to be central. My method was the same for every route: read both contracts, align the vocabulary, ask the same questions, label every claim by its evidence, then challenge the result in a critical review. That review changed some conclusions; appendix B lists them. Likely question: why not test the API? There was no test licence, and Horus requests run on real data.

slides.title: Nothing is ruled out, but only one route is fully confirmed
slides.lead: The documentation rules out none of the 11 routes, but most still rest on assumptions or open answers. Proposal: a short validation phase first, not a full build.
slides.callout: Not concluded for any list route: behaviour on large folders (no documented limits, no volume test run).
slides.notes: Here's the short answer. Horus has a documented endpoint for the core object of every route, so the documentation rules nothing out. But that isn't the same as everything being settled. Only analytic accounts is fully confirmed. Six routes are feasible but rest on assumptions the docs don't confirm. Four need answers from Horus or decisions from Chift; they are likely your clients' highest-value routes, which I'd confirm with you. For every list route, I can't conclude how it behaves on large folders. Hence my proposal: a short validation phase, not a full build. Likely question: 'So is it feasible?' Nothing is blocked, but four designs aren't final yet.

slides.title: Core capabilities are documented; VAT, read rules and volumes are not
slides.lead: Every claim is sorted by its evidence: stated in the documentation, assumed, owned by someone to answer, or not yet decidable.

items.text: Every route has documented Horus endpoints for its core object
Invoices and credit notes post natively, with VAT, analytics and PDF in one call
Client open items are native, with open amount and payment status
Lists return complete results, so paging can be emulated
VAT spreadsheets are current, and the API accepts the Luxembourg origins
Invoice or credit note on read follows the daybook type (proposed rule)
Horus, VAT and posting: tax files, credit notes, numbering
Horus, reads: ledger currency, limits, partial matching
Chift: posting mode, unnumbered invoices, caching, currency conversion
Performance and completeness of list routes on large folders
Supplier open items for partly paid invoices (depends on H8)
Whether every VAT case can be expressed, e.g. non-VAT-liable folders

slides.callout: Also before build: Horus registration, test licence, API addresses, confirmation rights, documentation version (H19, H17, H24, H21, H20).
slides.notes: This slide sorts the evidence into four levels. First, what the documentation states: endpoints for every route, native invoice posting, native client open items. Second, what rests on my assumptions; for example, that lists return complete results, which I deduced from the absence of paging parameters. Third, questions with an owner: Horus on VAT, credit notes, numbering, currency, limits and partial matching; Chift on posting mode, numbering, caching and currency conversion. Horus access, such as registration and a test licence, is also before build. Last, what I can't conclude yet. Incremental sync and the apiary documentation the case links are also open. Likely question: 'What's riskiest?' VAT, and the supplier side of outstanding items.

slides.title: One Chift call often means several Horus calls
slides.kicker: How Horus differs · Worked example: invoice creation
slides.lead: Horus needs its own references first, and a create returns only an id, so the connector looks up, checks, posts and reads back.

blocks.heading: Look up references, cached per folder

items.text: Why: Horus posts by its own codes; folder legislation selects the VAT list

blocks.heading: Check the partner's folder and role

items.text: Why: Horus needs a valid CompanyId before it accepts an invoice
Why: no idempotency key, and invoices cannot be deleted through the API

blocks.heading: Post to the sales or purchase endpoint, PDF included

items.text: Why: one native call per invoice or credit note; Horus returns only an id
Why: stored number, status and update date come only from Horus

slides.callout: Same pattern on reads: no endpoint lists all invoices, so invoice retrieval is rebuilt from ledger data.
slides.notes: This is the pattern behind most routes, shown on invoice creation. Chift sends one request. Before posting, the connector needs Horus's own references: the daybook, the accounts, the analytic codes, and the folder's legislation, which selects the VAT list. Those are cached per folder, but fiscal years are read fresh, because the accountant can close a period at any time. Then it checks the partner and, as a best-effort proposal, whether the number already exists. The create returns only an id, so we read the entry back. Likely question: 'Why so many calls?' Most are cached reference data, and a wrong invoice can't be deleted through the API, so checking first is cheaper.

slides.lead: Horus has its own vocabulary and rules; most effort and risk come from these differences, not from missing objects.

slides.callout: In Horus, a 'company' is a customer or supplier inside a folder, never the folder's own company.
slides.notes: Most mapping mistakes come from words that look alike. In Horus, a 'company' is a third party the folder deals with, a customer or supplier, not the folder's own company. One record can be both, which is why Chift's force_merge fits well. A journal is a daybook, and its type decides which endpoint can post into it. Analytic plans are cost schemas, and Horus stores amounts on combinations, not percentages. There is no VAT-code entity at all. And pairing 'posted' with 'confirmed' is my proposal, not something the documentation states. Likely question: 'Why not map posted to confirmed directly?' Horus keeps API entries unconfirmed for the accountant's review; that's Chift's call, C1.

slides.title: Each route has a main Horus endpoint plus supporting calls
slides.lead: For each Chift route: the main Horus endpoint(s), plus supporting endpoints for reference data, checks and read-backs.
slides.callout: '+ N' counts supporting endpoints, not calls per request · filtered reads (.list) use POST, reads by id (.info) use GET.
slides.notes: This table answers Task A. For each route: the main Horus endpoint, and a '+ N' count of supporting endpoints for reference data, checks and read-backs. That count is endpoints, not calls per request. One practical detail: Horus filtered lists use POST with the filters in the body; simple reads by id use GET. The last column rates feasibility by evidence, using the weakest point that materially affects the route. The full details per route, what is confirmed, assumed and open, are in section 3 of the report. Likely question: 'Which route is simplest?' Analytic accounts: one documented loop over at most eight plans, and the only route the documentation fully confirms.

slides.title: Reference routes need only small adaptations
slides.lead: Five rest on an interpretation of undocumented Horus data; analytic accounts is the one route the documentation confirms.

blocks.heading: Reads: journals, chart of accounts, folders

items.text: Journals: one call lists every daybook; blocked and currency flags rest on assumptions (H14)
Chart of accounts: number, name, status native; account type is a computed estimate (H12)
Folders: id, name, VAT number, address native; currency (EUR) and active status assumed
Ledger account creation: number and name documented end to end; the type cannot be written
Analytic plans: one call; parent_id rests on undocumented MasterCostSchema; Free-type hidden (Proposal, C9)
Analytic accounts: documented loop over up to eight plans; no stored balances (C4)

slides.callout: Build effort (analyst's estimate): low for journals, folders, analytic plans and accounts; medium for chart and ledger accounts.
slides.notes: These six routes are the reference data most other routes depend on, and they need only small adaptations; most are a single Horus call, cached per folder. The ratings are by evidence, not effort. Five are 'feasible with assumptions' because part of the response rests on an interpretation of undocumented Horus data, such as the account type, the folder currency, or the parent of an analytic plan. Analytic accounts is confirmed; Horus simply stores no balances, and how to show them is a Chift question, C4. Effort is my estimate, to calibrate with you. Likely question: 'Why isn't the chart of accounts confirmed?' Horus has no account type, so the Chift type is computed from several sources.

slides.title: Four routes carry the effort and the open questions
slides.lead: All four need Horus answers or Chift decisions before their design is final; likely the highest-value routes (to confirm with Chift).

slides.callout: Proposal: build invoice creation and operations after the reference routes; ledger-based reads wait for Horus's answers.
slides.notes: These four routes carry most of the effort and most of the open questions, and they're likely the ones your clients care about most, which I'd confirm with you. Invoice creation is native in Horus, but VAT, numbering and posting status need answers first. Invoice retrieval is the most complex read: no endpoint lists all invoices, so we rebuild them from the ledger, and telling invoices from credit notes rests on my assumption. Miscellaneous operations have no currency field, so who converts is your decision, C15. For outstanding items, the supplier side depends on how Horus returns partially matched lines, H8. Likely question: 'Which first?' Invoice creation and operations; ledger-based reads after Horus answers.

slides.title: Most attributes map directly or with a transform
slides.lead: The effort sits in lookups such as the VAT code, values the connector generates such as the client search key, and fields Horus cannot store.
slides.callout: 'Not available' is not blocked: Chift decides whether such inputs are rejected or dropped (C3).
slides.notes: Task B goes down to every attribute and query parameter of three routes: client creation, invoice creation and outstanding items. Each bar shows how the rows split by mapping type. Most rows map directly or with a transform, meaning a format, code, sign or unit change. The effort sits in lookups, such as turning a Chift tax code into a Horus VAT combination; in values the connector must generate, such as the client search key, which is always a proposal; and in fields Horus can't store, like line quantity or extra addresses. 'Not available' doesn't mean blocked: Chift decides whether to reject or drop that input, C3. The next slides walk through each route.

slides.callout: Writes go to real data, and the API has no call to delete a company (test folder: H17)
slides.notes: For client creation, the key idea is that Horus keeps one record per third party, the 'company', flagged as customer and/or supplier. So a Chift client becomes a company flagged as customer, and force_merge adds that flag to an existing supplier. The flow is check, create, read back, build, because Horus returns only an id. The real business choice is the search key: Horus requires it, Chift never sends it, and accountants see it as the client's code. My proposal is to derive it from the name, but Chift should agree the convention. Likely question: what if a client is sent twice? Without a VAT number or external reference, there is no reliable duplicate check.

slides.notes: Invoice creation is native in Horus: one endpoint for sales, one for purchases, invoices and credit notes, with the PDF in the same call. The work is resolving references, translating VAT, turning analytic percentages into amounts, and handling fields Horus cannot store. Two details in the table: the account number is Direct, not Lookup, because Horus posts on the account number itself. tax_code is a Lookup: the connector decodes it into a Horus combination, which is the next slide. Likely question: why so many calls? A wrong invoice cannot be deleted through the API, so the connector checks references, the closed period and the number first. Most of that is cached reference data.

slides.callout: Fallback if Horus cannot confirm the files: start with a reduced VAT-code list (proposal)
slides.notes: This is the most important transformation. Chift sends one tax_code per invoice line, the id of a VAT code. Horus has no such code: each line carries a rate, an origin and a type, plus kind and condition on purchases, and only the combinations in two published spreadsheets are accepted; the counts are on the slide. My proposal is that the connector owns a VAT-code list per folder legislation and direction, and rejects unknown codes before calling Horus. The spreadsheets and the API reference disagree in places, which is why H1 is the first question for Horus. Likely question: why not use the VatCode Horus returns on read? Its meaning is undocumented, so that is part of H1.

slides.title: Client open items are native; supplier open amounts must be computed
slides.lead: The route returns a folder's open items for clients or suppliers. Horus covers both sides, but not in the same way.

items.text: Open sales invoices list: native open amount, due date, invoice currency
Joined with customer ledger lines for account and matching number
Items keep their invoice currency (C16, H4)
No purchase-side open-invoice list: only supplier ledger lines
Connector computes open amounts from unmatched lines (Credit − Debit)
Partly paid invoices depend on H8; otherwise a fallback ledger read

slides.callout: No Horus paging: the connector pages the full set (H5, C14) · Signs and currency are proposals (C5, C16, H4)
slides.notes: Outstanding items show the asymmetry best. For clients, Horus has a ready list of open sales invoices with a documented open amount; we join it with customer ledger lines to get the account and the matching number. For suppliers there is no equivalent, so the connector computes open amounts from ledger lines not yet matched. The documentation does not say whether partially matched lines are returned. If they are not, partly paid supplier invoices silently disappear, which is why H8 is a before-build question. The first test: one partly paid purchase invoice and one partly paid sales invoice. Likely question: one call per supplier? No, provided that leaving out the company filter returns every partner, also H8.

slides.callout: Withholding tax, the Dutch G/N split and a forced period have no place in Horus: rejected (proposal, C3)
slides.notes: This is the slide I would share with a client application team, because it translates the mapping into what they will actually see. The biggest frictions are numbering and review: a vendor used to 'posted' will see drafts until the accountant confirms, unless Chift chooses direct posting. Second, a pushed invoice cannot be deleted through the integration, and an edited one comes back with a new id, so matching on journal and number matters. The currency row is a proposal until Horus answers H4. Likely question: which is the hardest to explain to clients? Probably the new id after an edit, because it breaks stored references; a periodic full re-sync covers it.

slides.title: Five Chift decisions shape what the connector promises clients
slides.lead: C1, C7, C14 and C15 are before-build questions; C2 shapes the VAT design. Each proposal is a recommendation, not an agreed rule.

items.text: Push entries for accountant review, or confirm them directly?
Mode per connection, review by default; return the status actually stored
Confirmation is accountant validation; invoices cannot be deleted through the API
Reject non-numeric numbers? What happens to invoices without a number?
Reject non-numeric; an unnumbered invoice goes to review as a draft
Horus stores numbers as numbers and does not number API invoices
Cache per folder and between page calls? Which timeout applies?
Cache reference data per folder and results between page calls
Horus lists cannot be paged; without a cache, every page re-reads the period
Does Chift core or the connector convert operations to EUR?
Convert at the supplied rate rather than reject; original currency not kept
Horus operation lines have no currency field; Chift requires a rate
Accept a connector-built VAT-code list per folder?
One list per legislation and direction; null on read when ambiguous
Horus has no VAT-code list and accepts no VAT code on write

slides.notes: These are decisions I cannot make for Chift: they change what Chift promises its clients and how the connector behaves next to other connectors. For each one I give a proposal, so the discussion starts from something concrete. C1 is the most visible: Chift defaults to 'posted', while Horus keeps API entries unconfirmed for the accountant. C7 follows from Horus storing numbers as numbers. C14 and C15 are platform questions, and C2 decides the whole VAT approach. Likely question: why review by default? Because a wrong confirmed invoice cannot be deleted through the API, and review is how Horus is designed; direct posting stays available per connection.

slides.lead: The before-build questions for Horus, grouped by theme. Other questions shape one route's design or can be checked in a test folder.

slides.callout: Proposal: no build without a test licence, because the API runs on real data
slides.notes: These are the before-build questions for Horus, grouped so they are easy to send as one list. If I could ask only four first: are the VAT spreadsheets current, what are the limits and can we get a test licence, how do numbering and retries work, and how are partial matches returned for suppliers. The access questions come first in time, because registration and a test folder unlock every other check. Likely question: why is H20 there? The case links the older apiary documentation; I used the current docs and did not compare the two, so Horus should confirm which one is authoritative.

slides.lead: A short validation phase rather than a full build. The ledger-based reads wait until Horus has answered.

slides.callout: A proposal for Chift's decision, not a commitment on behalf of Chift or Horus
slides.notes: My recommendation is deliberately cautious. Gate 0 is cheap: send the questions, get a test licence, settle Chift's decisions. Phase 1 builds the low-risk routes that also prove the connection, the caching and the response times. Phase 2 adds the creates where VAT and numbering matter. Phase 3 holds the reads that carry most open questions. Throughout, the Task B tables serve as acceptance criteria, and every confirmed answer updates the detailed reference. The fallbacks keep the plan alive if answers disappoint. Likely question: how long will it take? I gave relative effort per route, low, medium or high, but no days: that depends on Chift's connector framework and on Horus's answers.

slides.notes: To close: Horus has a documented endpoint for the core object of every route, so nothing is ruled out, but only analytic accounts is fully confirmed. The effort and the risk sit in VAT, posting and numbering, and the reads rebuilt from the ledger. So my proposal is to validate first and build in phases. The concise report is the position I defend; the detailed reference holds the full mapping. Likely question: you changed your conclusion between versions? Yes. I reviewed my own work against the documentation and separated what is documented from what I assumed. The material corrections are listed in appendix B.
